newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Angola's UNITA moves to avert new U.N. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Angola's UNITA moves to avert new U.N. sanctions.

text.p: Former Angolan rebel movement UNITA, under mounting international pressure, has offered to hand over territory still under its control by the end of November, the Lusa news agency reported on Tuesday.
UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi made the offer in a telephone conversation with a senior U.S. government official on Monday, the Portuguese agency cited Unita as saying in Washington.
The United Nations had given UNITA, which reached a peace accord with the Luanda government three years ago, until August 15 to meet certain conditions or face further sanctions.
The peace deal, signed in Lusaka in 1994, ended nearly two decades of civil war.
But the treaty's conditions have never been fully honoured and in recent weeks the country has seemed to be lurching towards renewed hostilities, with reports of troop buildups and isolated fighting.
The United Nations has already banned sales of arms and fuel to the Angolan opposition movement and was threatening to extend the action to cover travel and banking.

According to Lusa, Savimbi offered to cede his remaining territory, which includes diamond-producing areas, in two phases, with the first to be completed by September 24 and the second by the end of November.

In return, the organisation wanted its Vorgan radio station, which President Jose Eduardo dos Santos has accused of voicing anti-government propaganda, to be given the capacity to broadcast throughout Angola.
Lusa quoted the Centre for Democracy in Angola, UNITA's representative in Washington, as saying that Savimbi detailed the positions and strength of troops under his command.
It could give no further details. United Nations officials rejected a UNITA assertion in late July that it had just 3,000 men under arms.

The Angolan government says that UNITA has around 35,000 armed men, while military analysts and diplomats in Luanda estimate the military strength of the former rebels at anywhere between 15,000 and 25,000 men.
Under the terms of the peace treaty UNITA was supposed to disarm completely and its forces merge with those of the ruling MPLA in a single national army.

But Lusa said that the UNITA officials made no mention of disarmament. It was not known whether Savimbi made any new commitments in his conversation with U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Political Affairs Thomas Pickering.
The UNITA proposals had also been sent to the U.N. special representative in Angola, Alioune Blonin Beye, Lusa said.
